Acrylic paint-along · beginner

A small red sailboat with a white sail on teal water at sunset

Start on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

16 stepsCanvas: 16 x 12 inFocal point: the sailboat, with the sun and its gold path as the second point of interest Light: the setting sun low on the horizon, just left of the middle, so the light comes from behind the scene and from the left of the boatHow this lesson was made

Get these out of the box before you start. Every paint in the lesson is mixed from them; squeeze out a little of each when its step comes up.

What you need

Brushes

  • 1 inch wide flat: Blend the sunset skyFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • #6 round: Paint the sunRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • 3/4 inch flat: Lay in the far hill and shoreFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • 1/2 inch flat: Lay the first layer of the sun pathFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • liner: Line in the mast and boomLiner: long, very thin bristles, for fine lines like twigs and grass
  • #12 bright: Pull down the red of the hullFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • small round: Zigzag the mast's reflectionRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press

Also

  • A 16 x 12 in canvas, landscape (hang it that way). Using another size? Scale every measurement.
  • A ruler
  • Water jar and paper towel
  • Palette or paper plate for mixing

Placing shapes with a transfer outline optional

The transfer outline (optional)

The outlines of the main shapes, on a grid of quarters: 1 The sail; 2 The hull. On your 16 x 12 in canvas the grid lines are 4 in apart across and 3 in apart down. Before the stage that starts one, you can lightly chalk its outline on the canvas, measuring from the edges with a ruler.

Each one's card is open in the step that first uses it.

Getting started

The other basics are in the steps where they matter.

Before you start

Not checked yet

  • Two water jars: one to rinse the brush, one kept clean for thinning paint. A big clear jar shows when the rinse water is dirty.
  • A rag or paper towel, to wipe the brush between colors.
  • Put out bigger puddles of paint than you think you need. Big puddles stay wet longer than small smears.
  • Lay your colors out the same way every time, so they're easy to find and don't get dragged into each other.

Keep your colors clean

Not checked yet

  • Wipe the brush on a rag between colors.
  • Rinse it fully before going into white.
  • Rinse often. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  • Mix on the palette, not on the canvas. Two or three colors at most: stop when the color is right.

Keep paint from drying on the palette

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic on a brushstroke stays wet for only a few minutes.
  • Mist the palette lightly with a spray bottle now and then. Only lightly: too much water weakens the paint.
  • Cover the paint when you aren't using it.

Paint thickness and how much is on the brush

Not checked yet

  • Each step's Load line says two different things. How thick the paint is, and how much of it is on the brush. Creamy paint can be a full load or a light one.

How thick the paint is

How much is on the brush

How much water

Not checked yet

  • Keep water to about half the mix or less. More than that makes weak, see-through color that can lift when you paint over it.
  • For covering, use the paint thick, with little or no water.
  • After rinsing, wipe the metal part of the brush dry.
If something goes wrong not checked yet

Fixing a mistake

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic is forgiving. Let the area dry, then paint over it and try again.
  • Don't keep working a spot that's half dry. Leave it, work somewhere else, and come back.

The sunset sky 2 steps

STEP 1 OF 16 · The sunset sky, 1 of 2

Blend the sunset sky

  1. Inside the outlined area, all the way across from the top edge. Its bottom is about 6 in from the bottom edge.
  2. Paint a little past its bottom, under where the far hill and shore, and the sun path will go.
  3. Paints, top to bottom: Lavender purple, Sunset pink, then Sunset orange.
  4. Brush: 1 inch wide flat. Load: Creamy paint. An even coat.
  5. Start with the darkest color and stroke side to side. Without rinsing, pick up the next lighter color and paint below it. Then stroke back up over the join several times.
  6. It should leave smooth bands of color, with a soft join where two wet colors meet.
  7. Watch out: Blending after the paint has started to drag. Acrylic sets in minutes, and scrubbing setting paint lifts it and leaves streaks. Fix: stop as soon as it drags.
  8. Let it dry, then blend a new thin layer on top.

Tip: The light comes from the setting sun, low on the horizon just left of the middle, so the sky is brightest orange there and turns pink, then lavender, toward the top. Lay the lavender across the top, the pink below it, and the orange from about the middle down to past the horizon, then blend each join while wet.

Stroke: Side-to-side blend how to do it here, adapted for this painting, not checked yet

Side-to-side blend

Adapted for this painting from the Side-to-side blend card, not checked yet

The general Side-to-side blend card (its file)

With. wide flat; 3/4 inch wash brush

Load. Creamy paint. An even coat.

Motion. Start with the lavender purple across the top and stroke side to side. Without rinsing, pick up the sunset pink and paint below it, then the sunset orange below that. Then stroke back up over each join several times.

What it leaves. Smooth bands of lavender, pink, and orange, with a soft join where two wet colors meet.

Then. Stroke back over each join while it's wet, so the pink melts into the lavender above and the orange below.

Blend the sunset bands side to side

Dashed outline: what to paint in that picture. Arrows: which way to move the brush.

If it goes wrong.

  • A hard line where the pink meets the lavender or the orange. Add more of the lighter color at that join and blend again.
  • The lavender and the orange won't blend. That is what the sunset pink is for: it's the bridge color between them, so paint it between the two and blend each join.
  • The brush is overloaded. Wipe it on a rag. Rinse before going into a lighter color.
The general Side-to-side blend card

Not checked yet

With. wide flat; 3/4 inch wash brush

Load. Creamy paint. An even coat.

Motion. Start with the darkest color and stroke side to side. Without rinsing, pick up the next lighter color and paint below it. Then stroke back up over the join several times.

What it leaves. Smooth bands of color, with a soft join where two wet colors meet.

Then. Stroke back over each join while it's wet.

Blend two colors side to side

Dashed outline: what to paint in that picture. Arrows: which way to move the brush.

If it goes wrong.

  • A hard line where two colors meet. Add more of the lighter color at the join and blend again.
  • Two very different colors won't blend. Mix a bridge color from the two on the palette (pink and yellow make orange) and paint it between them.
  • The brush is overloaded. Wipe it on a rag. Rinse before going into white.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 2 OF 16 · The sunset sky, 2 of 2

Paint the sun

  1. Let the sunset sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush fully first: this is the lightest paint yet.
  3. Inside the outlined area. Its top is about 4 1/2 in from the top edge, and its left side is about 7 1/2 in from the left edge; it's about 3/4 in wide and 3/4 in tall.
  4. Paint: Pale sun yellow.
  5. Brush: #6 round.
  6. Small circles with the tip of the brush, from the middle of the sun out to its round edge.
  7. It should leave a round sun with a soft, slightly bumpy edge.
  8. Watch out: The edge is too hard. Fix: soften it with lighter passes. Smudging with a finger works too.
  9. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: The sun is a circle about 3/4 inch across, sitting just above where the far hill's slope meets the horizon line. Keep it a clean round shape: work the small circles from its middle outward to the edge.

  • Between steps, the paint underneath should be dry to the touch. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.

The far hill 1 step

STEP 3 OF 16 · The far hill, 1 of 1

Lay in the far hill and shore

  1. Let the sunset sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush well first. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  3. Inside the outlined area, all the way across. Its top is about 5 in from the top edge and its bottom is about 5 1/2 in from the bottom edge.
  4. Paint: Far hill purple.
  5. Brush: 3/4 inch flat.
  6. Keep the brush level and the strokes long, left and right.
  7. It should leave flat, level bands that seem to stretch away, with slight streaks that follow the stroke.
  8. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: The hill rises from the left edge to a soft round top about 2 inches in, then slopes gently down to the right until it becomes a thin flat band of shore that runs all the way across behind the sun and the boat. Paint the slope with the stroke following it, then the band in long level strokes.

The water 1 step

STEP 4 OF 16 · The water, 1 of 1

Lay in the teal water

  1. Let the far hill and the sunset sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area, all the way across to the bottom edge. Its top is about 5 1/2 in from the bottom edge.
  3. Paint: Deep teal.
  4. Brush: 1 inch wide flat. Load: Creamy paint. An even coat.
  5. Stroke side to side across the whole water, left to right, overlapping each stroke a little with the one above.
  6. It should leave level bands of teal, with slight streaks that follow the stroke.
  7. Watch out: A hard line where strokes meet. Fix: stroke back over the join while the paint is wet.
  8. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: Paint straight across where the sun path and the boat's reflection will go; they go on later over the dry teal. Keep every stroke level, left to right, and let a few loose streaks show: they read as gentle ripples.

The sun path 2 steps

STEP 5 OF 16 · The sun path, 1 of 2

Lay the first layer of the sun path

  1. Let the water and the far hill dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. Its bottom is about 3/4 in from the bottom edge, and its left side is about 1 1/2 in from the left edge; it's about 9 1/2 in wide and 5 in tall.
  3. Paints, darkest first: Soft gray-teal, then Muted gold. The paint map shows where each goes.
  4. Mix enough Soft gray-teal for this step and step 16; cover it between them.
  5. Mix enough Muted gold for this step and step 12; cover it between them.
  6. Brush: 1/2 inch flat. Load: Creamy paint, a light load.
  7. Short, level dashes. Small and close together at the top of the area, longer and wider apart lower down.
  8. It should leave short, flat, level marks with gaps of the color underneath between them.
  9. Watch out: The dashes smear into the paint underneath. That paint is still wet. Fix: paint them over a dry layer only.

Tip: Start right under the sun at the horizon, where the path is narrowest, and work down: the dashes get longer and the path wider toward the bottom of the canvas. The soft gray-teal goes on the outer edges of the path, the muted gold nearer its middle.

STEP 6 OF 16 · The sun path, 2 of 2

Brighten the middle of the sun path

  1. Let the sun path and the water dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. Its bottom is about 3/4 in from the bottom edge, and its left side is about 1 1/2 in from the left edge; it's about 9 1/2 in wide and 5 in tall.

The sailboat 6 steps

STEP 7 OF 16 · The sailboat, 1 of 6

Block in the red hull

  1. Let the water dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Optional: lightly chalk its outline first, from the transfer outline in Before you start, measuring from the canvas edges with a ruler.
  3. Inside the outlined area. Its bottom is about 4 1/2 in from the bottom edge, and its right side is about 1 1/2 in from the right edge; it's about 3 in wide and 3/4 in tall.
  4. Paint: Boat red.
  5. Mix enough Boat red for this step and step 13; cover it between them.
  6. Brush: 1/2 inch flat.
  7. Start with one simple shape, a long rectangle. Then add the curved pieces: the bottom curved like a shallow smile, and the bow on the right swept up to a point.
  8. It should leave a long red half-moon, flat on top, with small overlaps where the pieces join.

Tip: The hull is about 3 inches long and less than an inch tall: a long rectangle first, with the bow (the right end) pointed up a little, then curve the bottom edge like a shallow smile. Its top edge sits just below the dark shoreline band. Lay the red in strokes running along the hull, bow to stern, so the brush marks follow the boat.

Building from pieces

Adapted for this painting from the Building from pieces card, not checked yet

The general Building from pieces card (its file)

Motion. Start with one simple shape, a long rectangle for the middle of the hull. Then add the curved pieces at each end: a short rounded stern on the left and a longer bow on the right that sweeps up to a point.

What it leaves. A long red half-moon made of a rectangle and two curved ends, with small overlaps where the pieces meet.

Then. Soften where the pieces meet so the hull reads as one smooth shape.

Why a diagram: A shaped object (the hull) appears whole in one step, and a long half-moon with a raised bow is hard to start freehand.

Checked against the picture: Matches step 7's picture: about four times as long as tall, flat top, pointed bow on the right.

STEP 8 OF 16 · The sailboat, 2 of 6

Block in the sail

  1. Let the hull and the water dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush well first. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  3. Optional: lightly chalk its outline first, from the transfer outline in Before you start, measuring from the canvas edges with a ruler.
  4. Inside the outlined area. Its top is about 3 1/2 in from the top edge, and its right side is about 1 3/4 in from the right edge; it's about 2 1/2 in wide and 3 1/2 in tall.
  5. Paint: Sail shadow gray.
  6. Brush: 1/2 inch flat.
  7. Start with one simple shape, the tall right-hand triangle. Then add the narrower left triangle beside it, meeting it at the top, so they join into one tall gray sail.
  8. It should leave one tall flat gray triangle, its bottom resting just above the hull.

Tip: The sail is two triangles that meet at a point at the top: a narrow one on the left, a wider one on the right. Paint them as one gray shape with no gap; the mast goes down the middle later. The bottom stops just above the hull, with a sliver of water showing at the right.

Basics: Making a color lighter or darker

Making a color lighter or darker

Not checked yet

  • To lighten: add the color to the white a little at a time, not white to the color.
  • White also dulls a color. Too much turns it chalky.
  • To darken: add the dark into the lighter mix in small amounts.
  • For the next lighter value of something, start from the mix you already have and add white, so the colors stay related.

Light the sail

STEP 10 OF 16 · The sailboat, 4 of 6

Line in the mast and boom

  1. Let the sail and the hull dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush well first. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  3. Inside the outlined area. Its top is about 3 in from the top edge, and its right side is about 1 3/4 in from the right edge; it's about 1 3/4 in wide and 4 in tall.
  4. Paint: Mast brown.
  5. Mix enough Mast brown for this step and step 15; cover it between them.
  6. Brush: liner. Load: Thin paint. Swirl the brush in water, then in the paint. Add water if the line skips. Reload often.
  7. Hold the brush upright, with light, steady pressure. Pull the mast in one straight line from the deck up, then the boom out to the right.
  8. It should leave thin, flowing lines.
  9. Watch out: Lines that feather or spread. Laid into a wet layer underneath. Fix: let the area underneath dry first.

Tip: The mast runs straight up from the hull's deck, a little above the top of the sail, between the two triangles. The boom is a short line from the mast foot out to the right along the bottom of the right triangle.

STEP 13 OF 16 · The reflection, 1 of 4

Pull down the red of the hull

How Claude read your photosubject, light, layers

Before starting

Subject: A small red sailboat with a white sail on teal water at sunset, the sun low over a purple headland, with a gold sun path and the boat's reflection on the water.

Found in the image: just the picture

Done: none

Why: The whole image is the painted scene: no bars, borders, captions, or surrounding room.

Fitted to your canvas

Canvas: 16 x 12 in, landscape

Done: crop

Left out: about 11%: a thin strip of sky and water at each side (more of the left side's open water and headland foot)

Why: No canvas was named, so fit-canvas picked the standard size closest to the 3:2 photo (12x16, chosen by default). A crop keeps the boat, its reflection, the sun, and the sun path whole.

Beginner version

What made it too busy: No tiny separate things apart from the boat, which is the subject. No texture of hundreds of items (busy measured 0.0% fine texture). No detail inside big shapes beyond loose horizontal strokes in the sky and water. About eight parts (sky, sun, headland, shoreline, water, sun path, boat with sail, reflection), within the 8-part budget at 192 sq in.

Changed: nothing to drop or merge

Why: The picture is already a simple painterly scene a beginner can paint; every answer was no.

Fine texture measured: the photo 0.0% of the canvas

A calm sunset seascape: a purple-to-orange sky, a low pale sun over a purple headland, teal water with a gold sun path, and one small red sailboat with its reflection on the right. The big areas are easy; what makes it is the sun path and the boat's broken reflection, so the lesson spends its later steps there, and keeps the boat's pieces (hull, sail, mast) separate and simple.

Subject: A small red sailboat with a white sail on teal water at sunset
Focal point: the sailboat, with the sun and its gold path as the second point of interest
Light: the setting sun low on the horizon, just left of the middle, so the light comes from behind the scene and from the left of the boat

What it saw, back to front

  1. Sunset sky
  2. Far hill and shore
  3. The water
  4. The sail
  5. The hull
  6. The mast
  7. The boat's reflection
Why this techniquePaint along, back to front
ChosenPaint along, back to frontStart on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

A calm sunset seascape of big flat areas (sky, far hill, water) with one small boat in front is exactly what the beginner paint-along teaches: blend the sky wet, lay the far shapes over it, then the water, the sun path, and the boat and its reflection last, back to front. It is the only technique with version 2 keys.

Passed onBlock in, then build up (acrylic-block-in-beginner)

It has no version 2 keys (no v2_step_range or v2_rules), and the owner picked paint-along for beginner acrylic; toning and a separate block-in add nothing to a picture of smooth gradients.

How the paint recipes were worked out15 paints, free

Paint doesn't mix like light on a screen: blue and yellow make green, not gray. So the recipes come from a pigment mixing model (Mixbox), not a guess. For each paint it tried every simple recipe from your tubes, up to three colors plus white, and kept the one that lands closest to the color in the painting. Delta E is how far off it lands: under 2 is hard to see, under 5 is close, and over 8 means these tubes can't quite make it.

    Mixer: 4 parts white, 3 parts ultramarine, 1 part red

  • Sunset pink Delta E 3.7
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 3 parts white, 2 parts red, 1 part ultramarine

  • Sunset orange Delta E 2.2
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 3 parts red, 2 parts white, 1 part yellow

  • Pale sun yellow Delta E 1.4
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 4 parts white, 2 parts yellow, 1 part red

  • Far hill purple Delta E 1.1
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 2 parts ultramarine, 1 part burnt sienna, 1 part white

  • Deep teal Delta E 4.9
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 3 parts ultramarine, 1 part yellow, 1 part white

  • Soft gray-teal Delta E 1.2
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 3 parts ultramarine, 3 parts white, 1 part yellow, 1 part burnt sienna

  • Muted gold Delta E 4.1
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 1 part burnt sienna, 1 part white, a touch of yellow, a touch of ultramarine

    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

Why the steps go in this order16 steps

Back to front: the sky blended wet first and run past the horizon, the sun on the dry sky, then the far hill and shore over it, the water, and the sun path on the dry water in two layers. Then the boat, hull first and sail above it, the mast over the dry sail, and the deck line last so the mast is already in place. The reflection goes on last, after everything above the water is dry: the red, the white, the mast's zigzag, then ripples across it.

  1. 1. Blend the sunset sky

    The whole sky first, blended wet in one go, run past the horizon so the hill and water go over it.

  2. 2. Paint the sun

    The sun sits on the sky, so it goes on once the sky is dry, before anything in front of it.

  3. 3. Lay in the far hill and shore

    The far hill and shore are the next layer back to front, painted over the dry sky.

  4. 4. Lay in the teal water

    The water base covers the bottom half before the sun path and the reflection go on it.

  5. 5. Lay the first layer of the sun path

    The first, duller layer of the sun path on the dry water, as the research's two-layer path says.

  6. 6. Brighten the middle of the sun path

    The second, brighter and smaller layer down the middle once the first is dry.

  7. 7. Block in the red hull

    The boat is the nearest object; its hull is blocked in first as the base the sail sits above.

  8. 8. Block in the sail

    The sail blocked in its shadow gray, the darker base the light goes over.

  9. 9. Light the sail

    The warm white on the side facing the sun, leaving the gray down the middle: the sail's second value.

  10. 10. Line in the mast and boom

    The mast and boom go over the dry sail and hull as liner lines.

  11. 11. Catch the light on the mast

    A thin light line on the side facing the sun.

  12. 12. Add the deck line

    The light deck line last on the boat, after the mast, so the mast foot is already in place (an earlier order showed a ghost of the mast).

  13. 13. Pull down the red of the hull

    The reflection only once the boat is dry: the hull's red pulled straight down first, nearest the waterline.

  14. 14. Pull down the white of the sail

    The sail's white pulled down under the red.

  15. 15. Zigzag the mast's reflection

    The mast's zigzag through the middle of the white, over the dry reflection.

  16. 16. Cross the reflection with ripples

    Ripple dashes across the dry reflection last, which make it read as water; this ends with the finished painting.

Where Claude drew diagrams2 steps, free

Every step was read as a beginner with only its picture and words. The two boat block-ins need to be built from pieces, so they got construction diagrams; the rest are fills, lines, or repeated dashes the words and the paint map make clear.

  • Step 7: Block in the red hull beginner check

    Noticed: A shaped object (the hull) appears whole in one step, and a long half-moon with a raised bow is hard to start freehand.

    Pieces: A long rectangle for the middle first, then a short round stern on the left, the bow swept up to a point on the right, and the bottom curved like a shallow smile.

  • Step 8: Block in the sail beginner check

    Noticed: A shaped object (the sail) appears whole in one step; where the two triangles join isn't obvious from the picture.

    Pieces: The tall right triangle first, then the narrower left one sharing its top point, joined into one gray sail; the mast goes down the middle later.

What Claude would do differentlyfor the next lesson
  • The first finish render turned the water bluer than the photo's green-teal; one redo with the photo as the second input fixed it.
  • Kuwahara simplify erased the thin mast at strength 2 and 3; meanshift strength 3 kept it, as the skill says.
  • The water and the hull each hold only one distinct color (paints --add found nothing), so the water's optional streak and ripple steps and the hull's shadow pass were left out; the hull's slightly darker bottom has no paint of its own.
  • With the deck line before the mast, build-steps flagged a ghost of the mast: the fill under the mast and boom inside the hull's full step came out as a mirrored red smear. Moving the deck line after the mast cleared it without touching the outlines.
  • Step pictures show the hull's run-under strip just below the hull (the top of the reflection) as a mirrored red pattern until the reflection's own step; it reads as part of the hull for a few steps.
  • No Agent tool was available in this run, so the step review was done in the same context (review_context: same).
  • The drafted sky paints line listed the colors lavender, orange, pink; it had to be rewritten to the picture's top-to-bottom order.
